source.title: Adaptive Gradient Methods at the Edge of Stability
source.authors: Jeremy M. Cohen; B. Ghorbani; Shankar Krishnan; Naman Agarwal; Sourabh Medapati; Michal Baďura; Daniel Suo; David E. Cardoze; Zachary Nado; G. Dahl; J. Gilmer

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure labels and equations are garbled by text extraction, but the relevant figure captions and Appendix F description are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Reports test error across Adam learning-rate and β2 settings, bearing on how optimizer conditions relate to generalization, but does not test the claim versions' specified comparisons or measures.
record.gate_note: The paper's main results concern training dynamics and sharpness. Figure 19 and Appendix F report Adam test-error trends; cited findings about adaptive methods and generalization are not this paper's results.
record.test_reason: The study reports Adam training dynamics and within-Adam test-error sweeps, but none tests V1–V8. It does not compare Adam and SGD on held-out performance, compare batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets, or measure magnitude-aware sharpness against generalization gaps. Related optimizer-generalization findings are cited rather than reproduced.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes Appendix F: smaller η or β2 tend to coincide with sharper solutions and higher test error, without establishing causation. The paper's main conclusion concerns adaptive edge-of-stability dynamics and Adam's ability to enter higher-curvature regions through preconditioner adaptation.
record.recipe_differences: Studies adaptive optimizer training dynamics and reports test-error trends across Adam hyperparameters; it does not reproduce the listed claim versions' interventions or measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Test error tends to be higher at smaller η or smaller β2 in both full-batch and batch-size-4096 settings.

fits_no_version.finding: For a Wide ResNet on CIFAR-100, smaller Adam learning rates or smaller β2 tend to coincide with higher test error in full-batch and batch-size-4096 training, evaluated when training loss first falls below 0.05.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adam hyperparameters affect held-out performance within this architecture and dataset at a common training-loss threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 7 and Figure 11 report that Adam generally reaches larger maximum Hessian eigenvalues than momentum at comparable training speeds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adam and momentum can select solutions with different raw Hessian sharpness at comparable training speeds; this comparison does not establish a held-out performance difference.

record.problems: Test-error trends are shown in plots without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The authors explicitly do not claim that sharpness causes the test-error differences.
record.rows_left_out: No results were left out. Figure 19 reports the four test-error sweep conditions; no precise values are available in the text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance-level random-label held-out performance.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected held-out performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer held-out performance, tuning breadth, and recovery through weight decay or optimizer switching.
Large versus small batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove a penalty.
Dropout interventions and their effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with train-test error gaps, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 19's caption reverses the hyperparameter trend stated in Appendix F and Section 6, and its panel references conflict with extracted panel headings. The record's trend follows the consistent prose. The 0.05 test-error checkpoint is explicitly stated in Appendix F; Figure 10's sharpness checkpoint is 0.1. Optimizer preconditioning is not V7's scaling of perturbations to weight magnitudes.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; random-label held-out performance.
Width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold and test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier test error.
Adaptive versus SGD or momentum generalization comparisons, tuning breadth, and the named recovery methods.
Large versus small batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout intervention and its effect on test error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness perturbation measure and its ranking of train-test gaps against other measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

relation.reason: Section 3 discusses prior adaptive-versus-nonadaptive generalization findings, but the study supplies no held-out Adam-versus-SGD comparison or other test of V1–V8.

tranche.reason: The study examines adaptive optimizer dynamics and within-Adam test-error trends. It neither tests nor uses a listed version; raw Hessian sharpness versus test error does not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gap.

source_check.notes: Figure 19's caption reverses the trend stated in Appendix F and Section 6: the prose reports higher test error for smaller η or β2. Panel annotations also conflict; identify conditions by batch size and swept hyperparameter. No precise test-error results are stated, and causation is explicitly unestablished.
